approved: National Commission for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People (Transitional Provisions) Bill 2026

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2026-02-11.14.1) to agree with the bill's main idea. In other words, they voted to read the bill for a second time and can now discuss it in more detail. ### What does this bill do? This bill was introduced along with the National Commission for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People Bill 2026. According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2526/26bd043), which is a document created by the parliamentary library: > *The purpose of the National Commission for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People Bill 2026 (the Bill) is to establish the National Commission for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People (the National Commission) as a statutory agency and the National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People (the National Commissioner) as a statutory officer, with the functions and powers to advance the interests of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and young people.* > > *The National Commission for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People (Transitional Provisions) Bill 2026 (the Transitional Bill) deals with transitional matters arising from the enactment of the Bill to support the transition of the National Commission from an Executive Agency to a Statutory Agency.*
Glenn Sterle The question is that the amendment moved by Senator Waters be agreed to.
Glenn Sterle The question is that the bill be now read a second time.

Argued that the proposed national commission would duplicate existing bodies and add bureaucracy without delivering practical improvements for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, and said the coalition would oppose the legislation.

Supported the National Commission for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People Bill 2026 and related transitional bill, arguing that an independent national commissioner would strengthen accountability, elevate children's voices and address persistent disadvantage in child protection and youth justice.

Argued that the National Commission for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People Bill 2026 should require governments to respond formally to the commissioner's recommendations. Moved an amendment calling for governments to raise the minimum age of criminal responsibility to at least 14 years, citing children's detention harms and the over-representation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children; the vote was deferred.
